Xing"}, {"authorId": "2309897086", "name": "Xue-Zhe Ma"}], "abstract": "Looped language models reuse physical Transformer blocks across logical depth, but established architectures entangle recurrence placement, input injection, and recurrent state organization. We isolate these axes in models trained from scratch at matched parameter scale, logical depth, and token budgets, and then test whether the resulting design principles transfer to resident- and active-parameter-matched Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. The prelude-recurrent block-coda sandwich architecture consistently improves performance on context extraction and reasoning-intensive tasks. Input injection primarily enhances knowledge retrieval and context utilization, whereas random initialization and separate H/L recurrent states provide mixed or negative returns. Taken together, these results favor the Huginn-style design: at the 730M-parameter and 336B-token scale, the complete Huginn architecture outperforms Ouro across all ten benchmarks. The advantages of Huginn over Ouro transfer to MoE models. At the 8BA0.8B (32BA3B when unrolled) scale trained on 500B tokens, Huginn outperforms Ouro on nearly all benchmarks spanning knowledge, reasoning, and coding, while also exhibiting more balanced expert routing. Under matched training and inference FLOPs, the Huginn-style model uses 75% fewer resident parameters than a 112-layer feedforward MoE baseline. Despite its smaller physical parameters, it outperforms the feedforward baseline on DROP and GSM8K, matches it on MATH500, and remains competitive on the other benchmarks."}}, {"citingPaper": {"paperId": "7f45541410a06eaa64c1108bd02e87dcea3b65bd", "externalIds": {"ArXiv": "2610.22807", "CorpusId": 293453206}, "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/7f45541410a06eaa64c1108bd02e87dcea3b65bd", "title": "On the Position Bias of Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Study", "venue": "", "year": 2026, "citationCount": 0, "openAccessPdf": {"url": "", "status": null, "license": null, "disclaimer": "Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22807, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use."}, "publicationDate": "2026-10-16", "authors": [{"authorId": "2310386299", "name": "Yi-Ning Li"}, {"authorId": null, "name": "Hua-Yang Li"}, {"authorId": null, "name": "Le-Mao Liu"}, {"authorId": null, "name": "Taro Watanabe"}], "abstract": "Recent studies have shown that position bias remains a critical vulnerability in large language models (LLMs), undermining both the integrity of multiple-choice evaluations and the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation. However, existing understanding of this phenomenon is largely derived from studies with limited model coverage and English-centric benchmarks, leaving the behavior of frontier models and diverse languages underexplored. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation of position bias across model scales ranging from billion-level to trillion-level parameters, covering both multiple-choice and multi-document tasks in five languages. Our experiments reveal that while position bias remains noticeable in small-scale models and Non-English languages, increasing model scale and employing standard Chain-of-Thought prompting significantly mitigate this issue. Moreover, we demonstrate that emerging \\emph{thinking models} with extended reasoning capabilities are nearly immune to position bias, suggesting a costly but general approach toward resolving this vulnerability."}}, {"citingPaper": {"paperId": "af5f049e055f0968bf1e23e8aadba315b9965e6c", "externalIds": {"ArXiv": "2610.21149", "CorpusId": 292981981}, "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/af5f049e055f0968bf1e23e8aadba315b9965e6c", "title": "From Observation to Intervention: Distilling Self-Generated In-Context Demonstrations via Executable Causal Intervention", "venue": "", "year": 2026, "citationCount": 0, "openAccessPdf": {"url": "", "status": null, "license": null, "disclaimer": "Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21149, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use."}, "publicationDate": "2026-10-15", "authors": [{"authorId": "2400506936", "name": "Min-Ming Ye"}, {"authorId": "2391650908", "name": "Min Liu"}, {"authorId": "2047998054", "name": "Hao-Ang Chi"}, {"authorId": "2457910512", "name": "Ci-Heng Wu"}, {"authorId": "2239891839", "name": "Nai-Yang Guan"}], "abstract": "Self-generated In-Context Learning (ICL) enables LLMs to synthesize their own few-shot demonstrations, often outperforming manual prompts. However, existing methods filter demonstrations by observation, assuming a rationale is high-quality if it leads to the correct output. We show such filtering suffers from \\textit{observational equivalence}, whereby both faithful causal rationales and spurious post-hoc rationales can yield same outputs and are statistically indistinguishable from observation alone. Inspired by independent causal mechanisms, we argue that faithful rationales imply \\textit{transfer invariance}, in which causal rationales should remain effective across logically similar samples. We instantiate this criterion as \\textbf{E}xecutable \\textbf{C}ausal \\textbf{I}ntervention for \\textbf{D}emonstrations \\textbf{D}istillation (ECI2D), which abstracts language rationales into executable programs and applies the causal interventions ($do$-operator) on logically similar samples, retaining only those demonstrations that imply transfer invariance. Experiments on math, logical and commonsense reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ECI2D consistently outperforms observation-based ICL while retaining far fewer demonstrations, with gains exceeding 7 points as the test distribution shifts."}}, {"citingPaper": {"paperId": "e0cdfa1ee16bdfb1bad129a5ce97b3003c7df751", "externalIds": {"ArXiv": "2610.21594", "CorpusId": 293004017}, "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/e0cdfa1ee16bdfb1bad129a5ce97b3003c7df751", "title": "LoopAhead: Speculating Ahead for Faster Decoding in Looped Language Models", "venue": "", "year": 2026, "citationCount": 0, "openAccessPdf": {"url": "", "status": null, "license": null, "disclaimer": "Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21594, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use."}, "publicationDate": "2026-10-15", "authors": [{"authorId": "2257393033", "name": "Zi-Xuan Liu"}, {"authorId": "2300093743", "name": "Nan Xue"}, {"authorId": "2376123190", "name": "Rui Bao"}, {"authorId": "2400135523", "name": "Yu-Hang Xu"}, {"authorId": "2298762306", "name": "Xiao-Feng Cao"}, {"authorId": "3213796", "name": "Jiangchao Yao"}, {"authorId": "2376145027", "name": "Zhi-Yong Chen"}], "abstract": "Looped Transformers improve parameter efficiency by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers. However, generating each token still involves sequential computation and repeated access to model weights, leading to high decoding latency. Recent pipelined self-speculative decoding methods reduce this delay by drafting tokens from early-loop predictions and asynchronously advancing tokens at different recurrent depths in the same batch, but they do not fully exploit early-loop features for longer lookahead and still spend computation verifying incorrect speculative branches. We introduce \\method, a speculative decoding framework for looped transformers that enables earlier drafting of future tokens and assigns complementary roles to different recurrent depths. A lightweight lookahead drafter (LAD) predicts multiple future tokens with early-loop states, and deeper-loop feedback helps decide which draft branches to continue and which to pause, while the full-depth model makes the final token decisions. LoopAhead achieves up to 7.82x decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding while preserving the target model's output distribution."}}, {"citingPaper": {"paperId": "502911ae6188df03ed35d4e28283c1ecb91067a0", "externalIds": {"ArXiv": "2610.21244", "CorpusId": 292981786}, "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/502911ae6188df03ed35d4e28283c1ecb91067a0", "title": "System1-Arena: Which Decisions Can Be Left to System 1?", "venue": "", "year": 2026, "citationCount": 0, "openAccessPdf": {"url": "", "status": null, "license": null, "disclaimer": "Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21244, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use."}, "publicationDate": "2026-10-15", "authors": [{"authorId": "2303847301", "name": "Tian-Yu Chen"}, {"authorId": "2155562050", "name": "Xin-Yang Liu"}, {"authorId": "2267244124", "name": "Ru-Yi An"}, {"authorId": "2284725540", "name": "Zhen-Dong Wang"}, {"authorId": "2257010071", "name": "Ming-Yuan Zhou"}], "abstract": "Large language models (LLMs) often make discrete decisions, such as flagging phishing or escalating to a human. System-1 models, such as Jev and the OpenAI Decisions API, return probabilities over options in a single forward pass, while System-2 approaches generate reasoning steps. Which decisions can System-1 models handle, and which require generative reasoning? We introduce System1-Arena, a benchmark that gives all models the same decision requests and scores their probabilities. It contains 92k questions across 105 tasks from 268 public sources, in four groups: text classification and knowledge, applied decisions, evaluation and control, and agent and action. It also includes 138 closed-loop environments, from web shopping and SWE-bench coding control to robotics, games, and driving; in real-time mode, the world evolves while a model decides. We evaluate 30 models: 7 closed LLMs, 13 open LLMs read at the answer token, and 10 System-1 models. The largest System-1 models match or exceed fast closed LLMs in non-agentic accuracy, with better-calibrated probabilities at one-quarter of the latency. A reasoning LLM is the most accurate, at about 70x the cost of a fast LLM. In closed loops, large open LLMs succeed most often (up to 32.9%); small System-1 models rarely succeed."}}, {"citingPaper": {"paperId": "295da5584720625e47517c4bcbf9dcabd3fa1a92", "externalIds": {"ArXiv": "2610.21679", "CorpusId": 293004198}, "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/295da5584720625e47517c4bcbf9dcabd3fa1a92", "title": "No Single Tokenizer Feature Reliably Predicts Downstream Language Model Performance", "venue": "", "year": 2026, "citationCount": 0, "openAccessPdf": {"url": "", "status": null, "license": null, "disclaimer": "Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21679, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use."}, "publicationDate": "2026-10-15", "authors": [{"authorId": "65844422", "name": "Antonio Lopardo"}, {"authorId": "2408645322", "name": "Luis Frentzen Salim"}, {"authorId": "2315987232", "name": "Shikhar Srivastava"}, {"authorId": "2316641705", "name": "Kevin Jiang"}, {"authorId": "2332894534", "name": "Mridul Sharma"}, {"authorId": "2257347764", "name": "Catherine Arnett"}], "abstract": "Tokenization is a critical component of the language modeling pipeline, but it is poorly understood. Tokenizers can impact downstream performance, but there is currently mixed evidence about which tokenizer features predict a better language model without requiring a full training run. In this paper, we analyze approximately 200 language models trained on nine different languages. We evaluate both models and their tokenizers and test whether there is a relationship between any proposed intrinsic tokenizer evaluations and model performance, as measured by a wide variety of benchmarks. Despite the quantity and variety of proposed intrinsic tokenizer metrics, we find that none consistently predicts downstream performance across model families, tasks, and languages. This motivates the need for novel tokenizer evaluation metrics and approaches. We propose novel linguistically grounded metric introduced in this work shows that new metrics can capture aspects of tokenizer quality that existing metrics miss, though their predictive power is likely to vary across model families, languages, and tasks."}}, {"citingPaper": {"paperId": "2386391dd38a63857fd7f17196d014b9eec7b4d9", "externalIds": {"ArXiv": "2610.22650", "CorpusId": 293452855}, "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/2386391dd38a63857fd7f17196d014b9eec7b4d9", "title": "The Ephemeral Cost of Switching Optimizers Across LLM Training Stages", "venue": "", "year": 2026, "citationCount": 0, "openAccessPdf": {"url": "", "status": null, "license": null, "disclaimer": "Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22650, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use."}, "publicationDate": "2026-10-15", "authors": [{"authorId": null, "name": "Xin-Yu Zhao"}, {"authorId": "2282540347", "name": "Davis Wertheimer"}, {"authorId": null, "name": "Ashutosh Sharma"}, {"authorId": "2353611283", "name": "Rameswar Panda"}, {"authorId": "28130078", "name": "P. Liang"}], "abstract": "Recent work suggests that switching optimizers between pretraining and subsequent training stages incurs a performance cost, but systematic investigation of this phenomenon is lacking. We study the mismatch between AdamW and Muon optimizers by pretraining 1.2B Llama-3 models from scratch while varying the proportion of updates taken with each optimizer, and similarly interpolating between the two optimizers during continued pretraining and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Surprisingly, we find little evidence of a meaningful optimizer mismatch penalty: final performance is largely explained by the independent effects of the pretraining and post-training optimizers, with downstream performance generally improving as the proportion of Muon updates during SFT increases. Although matching the pretraining optimizer can reduce forgetting during SFT, this does not translate into improved final benchmark performance. We further evaluate AdamW and Muon for task-general SFT of open-weight models, across the Llama and Qwen families up to 14B parameters, where Muon remains competitive with AdamW, despite these models having been pretrained with AdamW. Together, our results suggest that the choice of optimizer for post-training can be made largely independently of the optimizer used during pretraining."}}, {"citingPaper": {"paperId": "9a0825db85ed67af2ef9d9f6145c2fb39b03fa74", "externalIds": {"ArXiv": "2610.20993", "CorpusId": 292982757}, "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/9a0825db85ed67af2ef9d9f6145c2fb39b03fa74", "title": "One Bias Score, Two Factors: How Mitigations Affect Option Bias in Multiple-Choice Evaluation", "venue": "", "year": 2026, "citationCount": 0, "openAccessPdf": {"url": "", "status": null, "license": null, "disclaimer": "Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20993, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use."}, "publicationDate": "2026-10-14", "authors": [{"authorId": "2216442555", "name": "Hyunjong Ok"}, {"authorId": "2344700590", "name": "Minjae Park"}, {"authorId": "2294676593", "name": "Jaeho Lee"}], "abstract": "Reordering multiple-choice options can change a model's answer, an effect studied as selection bias (a preference for certain option letters) and as order sensitivity (changes in answers across option orderings). We connect these perspectives through the pooled selection-rate standard deviation (pooled SD), which measures how unevenly option letters are selected across questions and orderings. When every option of each question appears equally often at each position, the pooled SD is exactly the product of two label-free factors: the flip rate and the positional skew. The flip rate is the fraction of questions whose chosen option changes across orderings; the positional skew is the standard deviation of option-letter selection rates among those questions. Across 41 checkpoints and 12 benchmarks, the flip rate tracks accuracy and output uncertainty, while the positional skew tracks the estimated option-symbol prior. Prior correction for selection bias mainly reduces the positional skew. Aggregating each ordering with its reversal, a mitigation for order sensitivity, mainly reduces the flip rate. Both reduce the range of accuracy across correct-answer letters by similar amounts, but aggregation leaves fewer model-rank reversals. Applying prior correction before aggregation reduces both factors and further narrows this accuracy range. However, aggregation lowers the flip rate partly by settling questions on the same wrong option. We therefore recommend reporting both factors to distinguish mitigation effects, alongside accuracy to distinguish stability from correctness."}}, {"citingPaper": {"paperId": "48aa5ffb1c22cb0c56e023a7abc7488232213791", "externalIds": {"ArXiv": "2610.19741", "CorpusId": 292902002}, "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/48aa5ffb1c22cb0c56e023a7abc7488232213791", "title": "Does the Linguistic Register of Thinking Matter? Wenyan as a Compact Reasoning Register for Chinese LLMs", "venue": "", "year": 2026, "citationCount": 0, "openAccessPdf": {"url": "", "status": null, "license": null, "disclaimer": "Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19741, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use."}, "publicationDate": "2026-10-14", "authors": [{"authorId": "2291199148", "name": "Ming-Han Li"}, {"authorId": "2331371334", "name": "Guo-Dong Zhou"}], "abstract": "Visible reasoning traces of Chinese reasoning-oriented LLMs are typically written in modern vernacular Chinese, which may be verbose under limited decoding budgets. We ask whether the linguistic register of reasoning can be used to improve efficiency. We propose Wenyan Thinking, which emits intermediate reasoning in Classical Chinese (wenyanwen) while retaining a short direct-answer output. Starting from modern-Chinese reasoning traces, we rewrite only the reasoning field into wenyan and fine-tune Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 on the rewritten supervision. To distinguish register shift from generic compression, we construct a compact modern-Chinese control using the same source data, teacher family, base model, and SFT recipe. Across budget-sensitive evaluations on MMLU-ProX-Lite-ZH, CEVAL, and AGIEval-CN, Wenyan Thinking substantially reduces reasoning length and missing-answer rates under constrained decoding. Compact rewriting explains much of the efficiency gain, while wenyan consistently outperforms the compact modern-Chinese control on the primary benchmark and remains competitive across the additional benchmarks. These results identify linguistic register as a practical design axis for efficient visible reasoning in Chinese LLMs."}}, {"citingPaper": {"paperId": "81c3219ad1d8301d1c057ee4914a06cd906b9882", "externalIds": {"ArXiv": "2610.19705", "CorpusId": 292902454}, "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/81c3219ad1d8301d1c057ee4914a06cd906b9882", "title": "RouteWeaver: Weaving Mode Selection and Execution into Unified LLM Routing", "venue": "", "year": 2026, "citationCount": 0, "openAccessPdf": {"url": "", "status": null, "license": null, "disclaimer": "Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19705, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use."}, "publicationDate": "2026-10-14", "authors": [{"authorId": "2510719510", "name": "Xiao-Han Wang"}, {"authorId": "2215405494", "name": "Haozhen Zhang"}, {"authorId": "2491606953", "name": "Qing-Yu Liu"}, {"authorId": "2409196803", "name": "Tao Feng"}, {"authorId": "2391642530", "name": "Wen-Ya Wang"}], "abstract": "LLM routing dynamically selects and coordinates heterogeneous language models across diverse tasks. However, existing approaches are largely built around a predefined execution paradigm, such as single-round, multi-round, or agentic routing, which fixes how model calls are organized and limits adaptation to different query needs. We propose RouteWeaver, a unified routing framework that integrates these routing modes within a single LLM policy, jointly learning which mode to use and how to select models within that mode. To jointly optimize mode selection and within-mode execution, we develop COMET-GRPO (COordinated Mode-Execution Training), which decouples the trajectory-level advantage into separate signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, enabling more targeted credit assignment to each decision level. We further introduce progressive exploration, which gradually shifts training from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection, so that the router first learns how to execute each mode before deciding when to use it. We evaluate RouteWeaver across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall. RouteWeaver achieves an average accuracy of 61.4%, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, and outperforms all compared baselines in each of the five domains. Ablations show that both COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration are important for adaptive routing; without progressive exploration, the routing policy collapses entirely to single-round execution."}}, {"citingPaper": {"paperId": "136c5d6a48a3ba4789b6f87cf74f5fc13ff21b76", "externalIds": {"ArXiv": "2610.19561", "CorpusId": 292903614}, "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/136c5d6a48a3ba4789b6f87cf74f5fc13ff21b76", "title": "REWIND: Uncertainty-Guided Trajectory Repair for Test-Time Reasoning", "venue": "", "year": 2026, "citationCount": 0, "openAccessPdf": {"url": "", "status": null, "license": null, "disclaimer": "Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19561, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use."}, "publicationDate": "2026-10-14", "authors": [{"authorId": "2452464312", "name": "Yi-Cheng Ding"}, {"authorId": "2350626033", "name": "Meng-Yu Wang"}, {"authorId": "2338351732", "name": "Min Zhou"}, {"authorId": "2344003316", "name": "Meng-Lin Yang"}], "abstract": "An early mistake in the generated reasoning can constrain all subsequent reasoning. Repeated-generation methods, like MCMC-based approaches, attempt to improve output quality by sampling multiple generations, but their effectiveness can be limited by randomly selecting where to regenerate. On MATH500 with Qwen2.5-Math-7B, we find that incorrect responses have substantially higher mean token entropy than correct responses, with an average within-question relative increase of approximately 112%, suggesting that entropy can signal reasoning errors. Motivated by this finding, we introduce REWIND, a training-free controller that uses entropy dynamics to propose targeted suffix regenerations. Across three model families and five benchmarks, REWIND outperforms all baselines, with gains of 0.51-10.00 percentage points over the strongest baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of targeted, uncertainty-guided trajectory repair across models and tasks. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rewind-D310."}}, {"citingPaper": {"paperId": "fd524ff44d140c3ab040278e945efb83ec113b37", "externalIds": {"ArXiv": "2610.19443", "CorpusId": 292902285}, "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/fd524ff44d140c3ab040278e945efb83ec113b37", "title": "More Than Seeing: Vision as Scalable Anchors in Native Multimodal Pre-Training", "venue": "", "year": 2026, "citationCount": 0, "openAccessPdf": {"url": "", "status": null, "license": null, "disclaimer": "Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19443, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use."}, "publicationDate": "2026-10-14", "authors": [{"authorId": "2275801674", "name": "Haoyuan Wu"}, {"authorId": "2330083019", "name": "Ao-Qi Wu"}, {"authorId": "2329023651", "name": "Jia-Ni Hu"}, {"authorId": "2402677290", "name": "Bei Yu"}], "abstract": "Native multimodal pre-training trains a single model from scratch on text and multimodal data, enabling it to understand both language and visual inputs. However, how visual signals shape scaling behavior and support capabilities beyond visual understanding remains unclear. We investigate this question through controlled visual-content ablations across model sizes and training budgets. Specifically, we replace image embeddings with content-free padding token embeddings. Retaining visual content improves text prediction on image-text examples without materially changing the lowest text-only loss at a given compute budget, the optimal balance of model size and training data, or aggregate language scores. The relative multimodal loss benefit grows approximately as a power law of compute. To test benefits beyond understanding images, we evaluate spatial reasoning from text descriptions alone. Both conditions improve with model and data scaling. During training of the largest model, visual gains are most sustained in localization, navigation, and symbolic planning, which involve maintaining object configurations or composing spatial updates; gains in spatial relations, geometry, and physical commonsense are less consistent. These findings identify visual content as a scalable anchor for multimodal learning, with benefits that extend beyond visual inputs while preserving aggregate language performance."}}, {"citingPaper": {"paperId": "0bf5ac4670c52d20e8ecfc5fe5cd77a31b7f5d1f", "externalIds": {"ArXiv": "2610.19685", "CorpusId": 292903060}, "url": "https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/0bf5ac4670c52d20e8ecfc5fe5cd77a31b7f5d1f", "title": "Beyond Distribution Matching: Selective Margin Preservation for Supervised Fine-Tuning", "venue": "", "year": 2026, "citationCount": 0, "openAccessPdf": {"url": "", "status": null, "license": null, "disclaimer": "Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19685, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use."}, "publicationDate": "2026-10-14", "authors": [{"authorId": "2510683456", "name": "Yuxuan Wang"}, {"authorId": "2346123786", "name": "Guang-Xiang Zhao"}, {"authorId": "2375981210", "name": "Xin-Yu Tan"}, {"authorId": "2499363704", "name": "Ya-Hui Han"}, {"authorId": "2510745365", "name": "Xin-Xiang Yin"}, {"authorId": "2510650594", "name": "Zhong-Hai Wu"}, {"authorId": "2346665469", "name": "Xiangzheng Zhang"}, {"authorId": "2346059467", "name": "Lin Sun"}, {"authorId": "2347000102", "name": "Tong Yang"}], "abstract": "Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) changes logit margins among non-target tokens at teacher-forced prefixes.
